video_title: Why Trend Following Might Outlast the AI Arms Race | Mark Rzepczynski | Systematic Investor | Ep.423
gist: Mark Rzepczynski and Niels Kaastrup-Larsen argue that 5%-ish long yields are a return to normal (real rate + ~3% inflation + rising term premium), that Treasury and dollar convenience yields are eroding while France loses safe-asset status, and that market micro-structure (dealer capital, hedge-fund bond ownership, commodity inventories) drives trends. They close with research showing ML crowding shortens alpha half-lives, while trend following, which has no alpha half-life, may outlast the AI arms race.

themes.theme: Bond selloff as return to normal

insights.claim: Mark Rzepczynski argues the current global bond selloff is not an anomaly but a return to normality, and that the near-zero and negative-rate era of the prior two decades was the true oddity.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Do not anchor on post-2008 yield levels as 'normal'; higher yields may persist rather than mean-revert.
insights.quote: the current environment is a return to normaly >> and the oddity of of the bond market was the periods where we had rates that were you know in some case in Europe negative

insights.claim: Using a building-block framework, nominal yield = real rate (approx. natural rate of ~2-2.5% from growth plus productivity) + expected inflation (~3%) + a term premium, implying roughly 5-5.5% before any term premium, close to where long US yields currently trade.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Fair-value math suggests long US yields near 5-5.5% are justified by fundamentals, limiting the case for a big rally.
insights.quote: what should a nominal rate be? It should be equal to the real rate plus expected inflation plus some type of term premium or risk premium.

insights.claim: The Atlanta Fed GDPNow forecast for US third-quarter growth is above 3%, which Rzepczynski cites as evidence of a possible growth and productivity boom that would justify a higher real rate.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Strong growth argues against falling real rates.
insights.quote: If you look at uh the Atlanta Fed uh GDP now forecast, we they're having for third quarter is above 3%.

insights.claim: US inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for well over six years, and Rzepczynski expects it will not return to 2% in the near term even if it abates slightly, so ~3% expected inflation should be priced into yields.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Persistent ~3% inflation keeps a floor under nominal yields.

insights.claim: The term premium was near zero or negative while the stock-bond correlation was negative; now that the correlation has turned positive and bond volatility is higher, investors should demand a larger term premium further out the curve.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Positive stock-bond correlation undermines bonds as a portfolio hedge and steepens curves.
insights.quote: The stock bond correlation is more positive. There should be more of a term premium or risk premium.

insights.claim: Some ultra-long sovereign bonds such as Austria's 100-year bond issued during the low-rate era have lost about 80% of their value.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Illustrates the extreme duration risk embedded in bonds bought at zero-rate yields.
insights.quote: Some of those have lost 80% of their value.

insights.claim: A generation of investors who started careers around 2006-2008 has spent nearly two decades only seeing extremely low rates, creating a historical-context gap that leads them to view today's yields as abnormal.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Institutional memory bias may cause misreading of the rate regime.

insights.claim: Private-sector borrowers and consumers have cleaned up their balance sheets and reduced leverage, while public debt-to-GDP keeps rising per BIS-style credit-to-GDP early-warning measures, putting the vulnerability in sovereigns such as France and the US.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Sovereign credit, not corporate credit, is the locus of fiscal risk this cycle.
insights.quote: consumers and businesses that they seem like they understand how they how to manage their balance sheets and the public has not

insights.claim: Governments are failing to run primary surpluses after recoveries as countercyclical fiscal policy would require, and interest costs are becoming a major and growing share of the US federal budget, dwarfing many other spending categories; the same is occurring in France.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Rising interest burden creates a fiscal feedback loop that keeps pressure on long yields.

insights.claim: According to Jesper Koll (cited by the host from a prior episode), roughly a third of Japan's budget now goes to servicing debt after the rise in Japanese yields.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Japan's debt-service burden is a growing fiscal constraint.

insights.claim: Private markets are crowding out public debt markets because of the tremendous demand for new private debt financing.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Competition for capital adds upward pressure on sovereign yields.

insights.claim: Equity tailwinds like buybacks are fading and equity supply is rising, intensifying competition for capital.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Supply/demand for equities is becoming less supportive.

insights.claim: With central banks no longer buying via QE, hedge funds have become far more important holders of government debt via basis trading and financing, and their demand is much more price-elastic than official buyers'.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Bond markets are more prone to sharp moves because marginal holders de-risk quickly.
insights.quote: hedge funds >> are much more active in the debt markets through basis trading and fin uh financing

insights.claim: Multi-strategy pod funds that lose around 5% will cut positions even in arbitrage-like trades, so a shift in their expectations could cause either a big bond selloff or a big rally.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Expect two-way tail risk in Treasuries driven by leveraged holder flows, not just fundamentals.

insights.claim: Record demand at the latest 20-year JGB auction, almost six times oversubscribed, pulled Japanese yields lower and hurt trend followers' fixed-income positions in early Q4.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Short-bond trend positions are vulnerable to auction-driven reversals.

insights.claim: JGBs have probably been one of the best markets for trend followers over the past 12 months, after years as a 'widowmaker' short where repeated small stop-outs occurred.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Patience in persistent losing shorts can eventually pay off when regimes change.

themes.theme: Safe assets and convenience yield erosion

insights.claim: Treasuries earn a convenience yield because investors pay a premium for a liquid, deep safe asset, and that convenience yield rises in crises when demand for safety surges relative to supply.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Safe-asset premium is a key driver of Treasury pricing in stress.

insights.claim: Ever-increasing Treasury issuance expands the supply of the perceived safe asset, shrinking the convenience yield; it has likely disappeared at the long end and now resides mostly in Treasury bills.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Long-end Treasuries lose their financing advantage; the Treasury tilting issuance to bills follows where convenience yield remains.
insights.quote: what was perceived as a convenience yield has may have disappeared. It's mostly on the short end now which was in the Treasury bills.

insights.claim: Central bank reserve managers have reduced dollar exposure at the margin, and the dollar regime is moving toward multipolarity; the dollar's convenience yield as reserve currency is diminished in relative terms though not in jeopardy.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Gradual reserve diversification is a structural headwind for dollar assets.
insights.quote: the dollar regime is is breaking and there's more of we'll call it multipolarity

insights.claim: France can no longer be considered a European safe asset, and it is plausible that the southern periphery (Italy, Spain, Portugal, even Greece) is not as risky relative to France as previously assumed.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Watch for France-periphery spread compression or inversion in European sovereign relative-value trades.
insights.quote: is France a safe asset in by any stretch of the imagination?

insights.claim: France's 10-year yield is just above 5%, up about 1.65 percentage points over 12 months and half a point in the last month, a 24-year high, amid violent protests and riots.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: French sovereign stress echoes the euro crisis but now at a core country.

insights.claim: Social unrest in France affects how investors view safe assets and bond markets even if not visible day-to-day.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Political instability erodes safe-asset status.

insights.claim: Gold traded above $5,000 earlier in the year, dropped to about $4,100, rose to around $4,800 in summer, and is back near $4,100, off its highs despite safe-haven demand drivers.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Gold is not behaving as a reliable safe haven in the current regime.

themes.theme: Micro foundations and money plumbing for trend followers

insights.claim: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the economics Nobel for micro foundations of macroeconomics; Woodford's natural-rate and forward-guidance ideas shaped generations of central bankers.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Current central bank frameworks rest on Woodford's natural-rate concept.

insights.claim: Trend followers should study the 'micro foundations of markets' - who trades, exchange rules, how policy changes profit-maximizing behavior - rather than only price action.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Market structure analysis can explain why trends emerge in some markets and not others.

insights.claim: Markets with more hedgers relative to speculators, fewer profit maximizers, or heavy government involvement tend to offer better trend-following opportunities because trend followers take the other side of non-profit-maximizing flows.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Allocate trend risk toward markets dominated by hedgers/price-insensitive actors.
insights.quote: markets that have more hedggers relative to speculators, a trend follower could do better because you're you're taking the other side of uh of of hedggers positions.

insights.claim: Following Perry Mehrling's money view, a shortage of bank and primary-dealer intermediation capital (from repo stress or balance-sheet constraints) prevents warehousing of risk, forcing disorderly seller-to-buyer transfers and making markets more crisis-prone.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Monitor dealer balance-sheet capacity as an ex-ante indicator of crisis susceptibility rather than identifying crises ex post.
insights.quote: If you can't serve your warehouse function, then that means is that you're going to have to move from seller to buyer >> extremely quickly in a disorderly fashion.

insights.claim: The same intermediation dynamic applies in commodities, where trading firms act as dealers; liquidity shortages make participants scale in and out of positions, creating dislocations that become trends.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Commodity trader capital constraints can be a trend catalyst.

insights.claim: The old belief, associated with Victor Niederhoffer's paper, that trend followers could only profit when bonds rallied reflected the four-decade secular decline in rates from the 1981 peak; with a more two-way market, shorting bonds now works.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Trend strategies are not structurally dependent on bond bull markets.

insights.claim: Benign global economies may have been the cause of globalization rather than its result, and the pattern of benign periods punctuated by crises is the foundation of crisis alpha.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Calm regimes set up the crises that drive trend returns.

insights.claim: Peak globalization with low, stable inflation and rates coincided with a quiet, challenging period for trend following, according to the host.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Deglobalization regimes are favorable for trend.

insights.claim: The 1980s and 1990s contained many dislocations (Plaza Accord, S&L crisis, 1987 crash, ERM breakdown, Tequila crisis, Asian crisis) that the industry overlooks when it dates crisis alpha from the tech bubble.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Longer history shows crisis frequency is higher than recent industry narratives imply.

insights.claim: Rising geoeconomic fragmentation (tariff wars, sanctions, capital controls, industrial policy) should decouple markets and increase diversification available to trend followers, while less fragmentation raises correlations.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Fragmentation lets trend followers run more risk at the same portfolio volatility.
insights.quote: if the world becomes more fragmented and dislocated, >> we should sort of see the diversification increases in markets.

insights.claim: In a fragmented world with tariffs and sanctions, trading duplicate contracts (London and New York copper, cocoa, coffee; European vs US natural gas and crude) adds value because delivery points will diverge.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Expanding to regional duplicate futures may become a source of diversification.

insights.claim: When markets are divergent and correlations fall, trend followers can take more risk, which is why they often perform well in such periods; high correlation raises reversal risk.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Watch cross-asset correlation as a risk-budget input.

insights.claim: The real issue in commodities is inventory levels rather than production, because stockout risk makes users pay any price to avoid shutting down, producing nonlinear parabolic moves.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Track inventories versus 5-year norms to spot markets prone to explosive upside.
insights.quote: the real problem in commodities is not what is produced but it's what the inventories look like

insights.claim: European winter energy inventories are below the level of the last five years, so a genuinely cold winter could cause a stockout and a parabolic price move.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Upside tail risk in European energy this winter.

insights.claim: Fear of stockouts leads to precautionary hoarding that creates the very shortage it seeks to avoid, as seen in cocoa and in consumer runs before storms or during COVID.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Hoarding dynamics amplify trends into 'small-c crisis alpha'.

insights.claim: Markets with few close substitutes, such as diesel or cocoa, are most prone to stockout nonlinearities.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Screen for low substitutability when hunting convex commodity trends.

insights.claim: Underinvestment in commodity capex could be setting up another commodity super cycle, an 'upheaval' rather than a crisis, like the one that reversed in 2007-2008.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Long-term grinding commodity uptrends may be resuming.

insights.claim: Energy trends remained strong for trend followers, with energy up 2-3% on the day of recording.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Energy is a current bright spot in CTA portfolios.

themes.theme: Machine learning alpha decay vs trend following

insights.claim: Surveys suggest over 90% of hedge fund managers use machine learning to find alpha.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: ML adoption is near universal, raising crowding risk.

insights.claim: Research on the 'alpha half-life' finds widespread use of the same ML techniques (transformers, boosting) taught at schools like Carnegie Mellon and University of Toronto has shortened alpha half-lives through crowding.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: ML-derived edges decay quickly; expect rising compute costs to stand still.
insights.quote: the halflife of alpha has has has shortened.

insights.claim: 13F filings show increasing similarity in major hedge funds' stock positions, evidence that ML-driven strategies are 'eating their own'.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Crowded equity positioning increases deleveraging risk.

insights.claim: The crowding forces quants into a 'Red Queen' problem of ever-larger computing budgets to find new models just to stay even.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Arms race economics favor strategies not reliant on secret technique.
insights.quote: which is called the red queen problem

insights.claim: Trend following may lack an alpha half-life because it does not predict where trends go and accepts trendless periods as a cost of doing business, making it more enduring than ML alpha.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Trend following could outlast the AI arms race as a durable strategy.
insights.quote: The nice part about trend following is is that we may not have the same thing as a as an alpha halflife

insights.claim: Machine learning techniques offer no secret sauce because they are taught openly in schools and every quant hire uses accepted methods.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Edge must come from data or structure, not technique.

themes.theme: CTA performance and earnings vs discount rates

insights.claim: As of Oct 20, the SG CTA index was down about 1.25% in October but up about 14.25% YTD, the SG Trend index up 14.57% YTD, and short-term traders up 4.93% YTD; the host's trend barometer stood at 40 (lower neutral).
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Trend following is having a strong year despite a soft start to Q4.

insights.claim: World government bonds were down 2.19% YTD while MSCI World was up 13.3% YTD as of recording.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: CTAs are matching equities and beating bonds YTD.

insights.claim: Stocks keep rising despite higher discount rates because earnings growth has outpaced the discount-rate effect; once earnings momentum fades, the discount rate will dominate and equities face real downside.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Watch EPS momentum as the key support for equities in a higher-rate world.
insights.quote: Once earnings stop to increase, you lose earnings momentum. Then what we're going to sort of see that the discount rate will then become more dominant.
